title: How the game shows what you can use
summary: Supermarket Simulator tells you what you can act on rather than leaving you to guess: the game keeps a crosshair manager, a highlight system and a set of indicators for what you are holding.
body: The game points things out. There is a crosshair manager and a crosshair reference of its own, so the middle of the screen carries information rather than only aiming.
Things you can act on light up. The game keeps a highlight manager with highlightable objects and settings of its own, which is why a shelf or a box draws attention when you look at it.
Highlights are generated rather than hand-wired. There is a generator behind them, which is why new objects can join the same behaviour instead of each one being fitted individually.
What you are holding is shown separately. There is an indicator for the thing in your hands, which is why carrying something and looking at something are two different pieces of information.
Messages appear in words. There is an in-game text indicator, which is how the game tells you something in text rather than only in colour.
Limits have their own warning. A cart that is full has its own indicator, which is why you find out a cart is maxed instead of wondering why nothing else fits.
Objects opt into it. Interactable things share a common behaviour, which is why the same crosshair works across shelves, tills and doors.
What you can reach is gathered in one place. The wheel of tools is held by a controller of its own, which is why picking a held item is a screen the game can open rather than a list of keys.
Looking is a test with an answer. The game keeps a result for the ray it sends out and a result for what that ray met, which is why the highlight lands on the thing under the middle of the screen.
What this entry does not tell you: how far a highlight reaches, what each state looks like, or which objects are interactable. We have not verified those numbers, so we do not print them.

facts.claim: The game has a crosshair manager and a crosshair reference of its own.
Things you can act on are highlighted by a manager of their own.
Highlights are generated rather than fitted to each object by hand.
What the player is holding has its own indicator.
The game shows messages in text as well as in colour.
A full cart and a boost have their own indicators.
The build keeps a mode for highlighting of its own.
Interactable objects share a common behaviour.
The wheel of tools is held by a controller of its own.
The game keeps a result for the ray it sends out and a result for what it met.
Icons for the tools a player can use are shipped, a mop among them.
